title: Rutherford's Nuclear Model — Features, Successes and Drawbacks (Summary Tab)
topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: A compact revision summary of the nuclear atom — the six features, three successes and five drawbacks in tabular form, ideal for last-minute revision. The detailed experiment and limitations are in the main and companion tabs.
1. Atom is electrically neutral and mostly empty space.
2. A tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (r ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m) sits at the centre and holds ≈99.9% of the mass.
3. Nuclear volume ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ of atomic volume (r_atom ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m).
4. Electrons revolve in circular orbits; Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force.
5. Number of electrons = number of protons → neutrality.
6. Nuclear charge is characteristic of the element — the seed of the atomic-number concept.
• Explained the α-scattering observations quantitatively (including the sin⁻⁴ law).
• Established the nucleus and the division of the atom into nucleus + electron shell — the birth of nuclear physics.
• Led to Moseley's atomic number, the discovery of the proton (1919) and neutron (1932), and the modern periodic law.
1. Instability: an orbiting (accelerated) electron must radiate and spiral into the nucleus in ≈10⁻⁸ s.
2. No explanation of line spectra — a spiralling electron would radiate continuously.
3. No arrangement of electrons: shells, energies and electron numbers are unspecified, so periodicity and valency are unexplained.
4. Purely classical: circular orbits and a point nucleus are assumptions; no quantisation means no orbital radii or energies.
5. Ignores the neutron, electron–electron interaction and bonding — fails for multi-electron atoms.
confusion: ❌ Rutherford's model places electrons in fixed energy levels. ✅ That is Bohr's addition; Rutherford allowed any circular orbit.
❌ The model was rejected as useless. ✅ It explained scattering perfectly; it failed only beyond that scope (stability, spectra).

summary: A compact revision summary of the nuclear atom. Six features: the atom is neutral and mostly empty space; a tiny dense positive nucleus of radius ≈10⁻¹⁵ m sits at the centre holding ≈99.9% of the mass; nuclear volume is ≈10⁻¹⁵ of atomic volume (r_atom ≈10⁻¹⁰ m); electrons revolve in circular orbits with the Coulomb attraction as the centripetal force; the number of electrons equals the number of protons; and the nuclear charge is characteristic of the element, the seed of atomic number. Three successes: it explained the α-scattering observations quantitatively, including the sin⁻⁴ law; it established the nucleus and the division into nucleus plus electron shell, founding nuclear physics; and it led to Moseley's atomic number, the proton (1919), the neutron (1932) and the modern periodic law. Five drawbacks: instability, since a radiating electron must spiral in within ≈10⁻⁸ s; no explanation of line spectra; no electron arrangement, so periodicity and valency are unexplained; purely classical assumptions of circular orbits and a point nucleus; and no neutron, no electron–electron interaction and no bonding.
importantConcepts: Six features: neutral, mostly empty atom; tiny dense nucleus (≈10⁻¹⁵ m, ≈99.9% of the mass); nuclear volume ≈10⁻¹⁵ of atomic volume
Electrons revolve in circular orbits with Coulomb attraction supplying the centripetal force; e⁻ count = proton count
Characteristic nuclear charge — the seed of the atomic-number concept and of Moseley's law
Three successes: quantitative α-scattering including the sin⁻⁴ law, the establishment of the nucleus, and the road to atomic number, proton and neutron
Five drawbacks: radiating-electron instability, no line spectra, no electron arrangement, purely classical assumptions, no neutron or e⁻–e⁻ interaction
importantStatements: Almost the entire atomic mass lies in a volume only 10⁻¹⁵ of the atom's — nuclear density ≈10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
The nucleus : atom radius ratio is about 1 : 100 000, since 10⁻¹⁵ m against 10⁻¹⁰ m.
Rutherford's model allowed any circular orbit; fixed energy levels were Bohr's addition in 1913.
The model explained scattering well and failed only beyond that scope — on stability and spectra.
Nuclear density is nearly constant for all nuclei because R = R₀A^(1/3) with R₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.

keyPoints: Feature 6, the characteristic nuclear charge, is the bridge to Moseley's atomic number.
One-sentence essence: a tiny massive positive nucleus with electrons revolving around it, the whole mostly empty space and held together electrostatically.
The sin⁻⁴(θ/2) scattering law is the quantitative success of the model.
Rutherford announced the nuclear model in 1911 and published it fully that year.
specialNotes: Rutherford's model is not the same as Bohr's: only Bohr quantised the orbits.
The model was not rejected as useless; it was superseded because it could not explain stability or spectra.
Ignoring the neutron left isotopes unexplained, which is a defect distinct from the other two classical ones.
